description: We are Space Craft, a team that seeks to inspire in the new generations the passion in space exploration. For this we want to bring them closer to the real experience of controlling space missions. We aim to develop a mod for Minecraft that inspires interest in space exploration. We are looking for members who handle github, with soft skills, interested in learning exciting new topics. If you are new to learning software development, interested in video games and want to learn JOIN!
summary:
DOKI Rocket is a browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a lunar outpost over a five-day mission, turning real engineering trade-offs into hands-on decisions. Each day, players split limited solar power between life support (air and a greenhouse), radiation shielding, and a science lab. No choice is free, and the lunar night forces them to plan ahead. On day 3, a real solar storm from NASA’s DONKI database hits the base. After every consequence, the game asks “Why did it happen?” and explains the science, drawing on RadLab radiation data and OSDR astronaut health findings. A short pre- and post-mission quiz measures learning, and every data source is credited in-game. No download or account is needed.

It matters because Peruvian sixth graders outperform the regional average in science (UNESCO ERCE 2019), yet most remain below the level where science is applied to explain and decide, and by age 15 more than half lack basic proficiency (PISA 2022). DOKI Rocket helps children practice using science, not just memorizing it.
details:
ROJECT DETAILS - Doki Rocket : Misión Luna

Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer (NASA Space Apps 2026)

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Doki Rocket : Misión Luna is a survival game for children aged 7 to 12. The player commands a small Moon base, seen from above on a 10 x 7 grid. The goal is to keep a crew of 3 astronauts alive for as many days as possible and beat their own record. There is no fixed end: the days continue until the crew has to be rescued or the player decides to return to Earth.

Every day the player makes decisions that all have a cost:

- Energy: solar panels produce only during the lunar day. During the lunar night (3 out of every 8 days), the base runs on what was stored in batteries. Every module that is switched on uses energy. If consumption exceeds what is available, the last module switched on turns off by itself.

- Building: panels, batteries, air generators, greenhouses, a laboratory, a shielded shelter and cables cost materials. A module only works if it touches the power network.

- Crew work: the crew has 3 work shifts per day. Each shift can repair a module or go on an expedition to collect materials. An expedition costs oxygen for the suits, and during a solar storm it exposes the crew to radiation.

- Science: the laboratory produces science points. The player can trade them for a supply rocket from Earth, which takes 2 days to arrive.

- System wear: modules break down over time, more often as the days pass. Each fault cuts output by 25%. Repairs are hands-on mini-games: click away lunar dust on solar panels, click to patch air leaks, click to clear residue from the greenhouse, and press and hold to reconnect loose battery cables.

Solar storms come from real NASA data. Each game day advances one real day of a 62-day calendar from NASA DONKI (May and October 2024, with 31 solar energetic particle detections across 8 storm days). Mission Control warns about storms and lunar nights 2 days ahead. In Commander mode, its messages arrive one day late, as with real communication delays. The player reads a 7-day chart of real particle detections to decide when to switch on the shelter.

After each important event, a "Why did it happen?" question appears with options and a short scientific explanation. A 3-question test before and after the mission measures what the child learned. The final report shows days survived, the record, the real storms faced and which decisions led to the result.

There are two modes. Cadet (ages 7 to 9) uses icons, colors and 2-option picture questions, with no radiation system. Commander (ages 10 to 12) adds the shelter, radiation, numbers, the real data chart and delayed messages.

NASA DATA USED

- DONKI (solar energetic particle events): the real storm calendar and the chart.

- RadLab (DosTel1 dosimeter on the International Space Station): the daily dose for 59 of the same days. During the May and October 2024 storms, the daily average on the ISS stayed close to 20 μGy/h, because Earth's magnetic field protects it. The game uses this real result to explain why the Moon, which has no such shield, needs a shelter.

- OSDR studies OSD-342, OSD-396 and OSD-253: real findings on muscle loss, bone loss, fracture healing and daily rhythms in space, shown in the final report.

Every event is labeled "Real event of [date]" and is never presented as live. A Sources screen separates real data from game simplifications (costs, consumption, faults and lunar radiation values).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

In Peru, 6th-grade students score above the regional average in science (UNESCO ERCE 2019: 723 vs. 702 points). By age 15, however, more than half do not reach the basic level, and almost 8 out of 10 in rural areas (PISA 2022). Children learn science as facts to memorize, not as a way to reason and decide under limits. Doki Rocket makes them apply science: read a chart before deciding, explain why something happened, and understand that energy used in one place is missing somewhere else. Failure is not a punishment. The crew is rescued, the report explains the cause, and the open record invites the child to play again and try a better strategy. The before-and-after test gives teachers evidence of learning.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- HTML5, CSS and plain JavaScript, with Canvas 2D for the base map, walking crew and charts. No game engine or external libraries.

- JSON files for all NASA data and texts, plus a local JavaScript copy so the game opens with a double click.

- Python scripts to download data from the NASA DONKI and RadLab APIs and to package it. Only the team uses these scripts; the game does not need them.

- NASA OSDR search to select the studies.

- Visual Studio Code, and Microsoft Edge in headless mode for automated play tests and balance checks.

No special hardware is needed: the game runs in any modern browser on a computer, tablet or phone, with mouse or touch.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

- The storms are not random: the player lives through real solar activity, day by day.

- It contrasts real ISS dose measurements with the Moon's lack of protection, turning a data finding into a game decision.

- Repairs are physical mini-games that match each real problem: dust, leaks, residue and loose cables.

- Mission Control's delayed messages make communication lag something the player has to plan around.

- Survival with a personal record replaces "you lose" with "how far can you get".

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Access: many Peruvian schools, especially rural ones, have slow or no internet. The game works completely offline from local files, with no installation, accounts or downloads.

- Age: two modes, short sentences (15 words or fewer), and a glossary for words like radiation, dose and Sun.

- Cognitive load: 2 or 3 main resources on screen at a time.

- Honesty with data: dates are always shown, nothing is presented as live, and real data is separated from simplifications.

- No dominant strategy: automated tests showed that doing nothing lasts about 7 days and random play about 6. A simple careful strategy averages 23 days, with highs of 64 to 73. Better decisions give better results, but no strategy lasts forever.

- Accessibility: large buttons, keyboard support for the hold-to-connect action, high contrast, and reduced motion when the device requests it.

USE OF AI

The team used an AI coding assistant (Kiro) to help write code, process NASA data and run automated tests. The game design, problem analysis and decisions were made by the team.
